blocks.content: A {{term:regelkarte|control chart}} (SPC chart) plots a process metric over time together with statistical limits. It separates random variation ({{term:zufallsursache|common causes}}, process “in control”) from systematic deviations (special causes) and is the standard Control-phase tool to keep an improved process in check long-term.

The {{term:mittellinie|center line CL}} is the {{term:mittelwert|mean}} of the baseline points: the individual values, the subgroup means or, on the dispersion chart, the ranges or standard deviations. It represents the current process level.

{{term:regelgrenze|UCL and LCL}} are the upper and lower control limits, at 3 σ̂ from the center line. σ̂ is the spread within subgroups estimated from the data (from the moving ranges for individual values), not the {{term:standardabweichung|standard deviation}} of all values. Deviations within are treated as random; points outside indicate a special cause.

The region between center line and limits is divided into three {{term:sigma-zonen|zones}} of one σ̂ each: C up to 1σ, B from 1σ to 2σ, A from 2σ to 3σ. {{term:nelson-regeln|Western Electric and Nelson rules}} use these zones to detect non-random patterns.

A {{term:sonderursache|special cause}} is an influence outside normal process variation, e.g. a tool break, a new operator, a material change. It must be identified and removed before the process continues.

This module computes {{term:i-mr-chart|I-MR}} for individual values and {{term:xbar-r-chart|X̄-R}} and X̄-S for {{term:subgruppe|subgroups}}. For proportions (defective/not) there are the {{term:p-chart|p and np charts}}, for counts (defects per unit) the {{term:c-chart|c and u charts}}, both in the module Control Chart (Attribute). The choice depends on data type and subgroups.
Control charts prevent processes from drifting unnoticed. They are not quality verdicts but early-warning systems: they show something is happening before the spec is violated.

Each chart type consists of two subcharts: on top the location (individual values or means), below the spread (moving {{term:spannweite|range}}, range or standard deviation). The limits are computed from the baseline; the constants depend on the subgroup size n (section Constants).

Moving range MRᵢ = |xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁| of consecutive values. Individuals chart: CL = x̄, UCL/LCL = x̄ ± 3 · MR̄/d₂ = x̄ ± 2.660 · MR̄ with d₂ = 1.128, σ̂ = MR̄/1.128. MR chart: CL = MR̄, UCL = D₄ · MR̄ = 3.267 · MR̄, LCL = 0. For measurements that arrive one at a time (batches, daily values, costly tests).

Every n consecutive values form a subgroup with mean x̄ⱼ and range Rⱼ = max − min. X̄ chart: CL = x̄̄, UCL/LCL = x̄̄ ± A₂ · R̄, σ̂ = R̄/(d₂ · √n). R chart: CL = R̄, UCL = D₄ · R̄, LCL = D₃ · R̄. The range is easy to compute but loses efficiency as n grows.

blocks.term: X̄-S (mean and standard deviation, n = 2 to 25)
blocks.content: Like X̄-R, but with the standard deviation sⱼ of each subgroup (divisor n − 1). X̄ chart: CL = x̄̄, UCL/LCL = x̄̄ ± A₃ · S̄, σ̂ = S̄/(c₄ · √n). S chart: CL = S̄, UCL = B₄ · S̄, LCL = B₃ · S̄. From about n = 10 the better choice, because S uses all values of the subgroup.

Subgroups are formed from consecutive values of the column; values at the end that do not fill a subgroup are ignored. A subgroup should be taken under conditions as alike as possible (in quick succession, same machine), so that its spread shows the short-term process variation.

The limit factors depend only on n and come from the usual tables for control charts {{ref:montgomery-sqc-6|(Montgomery)}}. A₂ = 3/(d₂ · √n) and A₃ = 3/(c₄ · √n); D₃, D₄, B₃ and B₄ place the dispersion chart limits at ±3σ of the range or standard deviation, bounded below by 0. The module computes up to n = 25 with the same tables; the values up to n = 10 are shown here.
D₃ is 0 up to n = 6, B₃ up to n = 5: for small subgroups the dispersion chart has no lower limit, so a conspicuously small spread cannot be detected there with rule 1.

When a process has been deliberately retuned (tool change, new batch, material switch, machine override), global limits produce a misleading picture: they mix the old and new variation. With stages each section gets its own center line and control limits.

In the “Stage boundaries” field, enter the number of the last point of each stage, separated by commas. Example: “12, 25” with 30 points yields three stages: 1–12, 13–25, 26–30. Boundaries that do not lie within the series do not count. For X̄-R and X̄-S the numbers count individual values; a boundary should be a multiple of the subgroup size, otherwise the split subgroup is counted in the earlier stage (the chart warns about this).

The chart shows stepped center line and limits with dashed vertical separators at each stage break. Each stage is judged by its own limits: the Nelson tests run per stage and runs (e.g. test 2) restart at every stage boundary, on both charts. The moving range across a stage boundary is not plotted. The KPIs and Cp/Cpk describe the last stage, i.e. the process as it runs now.

Stages do not replace the baseline count, they are a different mechanism. Either use a baseline count (classic Phase I/II) or stage boundaries (multiple stable sections). When set, stages override the baseline count. With multiple stages exclusions have no effect and limits cannot be frozen.

The classic SPC workflow has two phases: Phase I collects baseline data, identifies special causes and excludes them until the baseline is “in control”. Phase II locks those limits and checks new data points against them.

The baseline count sets how many values from the start of the series the limits are computed from; empty means all values. The rules still check all points, so the values after the baseline are already judged against the baseline limits. For X̄ charts it is rounded up to whole subgroups; a number above the number of values means all values.

Click a violation row to open a dialog: record the cause as free text and optionally exclude the point from the limit computation. Excluded points appear as a gray ✕: they stay on the chart but no longer influence the center line, UCL and LCL. For I-MR the two moving ranges involving this point also drop out of MR̄. The limits update immediately after each exclusion. With multiple stages and with frozen limits an exclusion has no effect. The delete button in the dialog removes the annotation after a confirmation.

“Freeze limits” stores the current limits of both subcharts. Subsequent data points are checked against these fixed limits without UCL and LCL changing. “Thaw” returns to the live recompute mode. The limits belong to the column they were computed from: selecting a different column discards them. They also only apply with the chart type and subgroup size they were frozen with.
Phase II is only available without stages: multi-stage charts already have per-stage limits; an additional freeze would be double bookkeeping.

items: Pick the chart type by data type and subgroup structure: individual values → I-MR, subgroups up to 10 → X̄-R, larger subgroups → X̄-S.
Collect enough baseline data, typically 20–25 subgroups or 100+ individuals.
Compute center line and limits from the baseline (Phase I).
Check the dispersion chart first: if it is not stable, the limits of the location chart are not reliable either, because they are derived from the average spread.
Check for outliers and patterns, exclude special causes from Phase I and recompute limits.
Start ongoing monitoring (Phase II): each new point is checked against fixed limits.
On a rule violation, find, document, and eliminate the cause.
Recompute limits only when the process was demonstrably and intentionally changed.
{{term:nelson-regel-1|Rule 1}}: 1 point outside the 3σ limits — clearly out of control.
{{term:nelson-regel-2|Rule 2}}: 9 points in a row on the same side of the center line — level shift.
{{term:nelson-regel-3|Rule 3}}: 6 points in a row rising or falling — trend.
{{term:nelson-regel-4|Rule 4}}: 14 points in a row alternating up and down — systematic zig-zag, e.g. two machines taking turns.
{{term:nelson-regel-5|Rule 5}}: 2 of 3 points beyond 2σ (zone A) on the same side — near-limit excursion more often than expected.
{{term:nelson-regel-6|Rule 6}}: 4 of 5 points beyond 1σ (zone B or A) on the same side — small shift of the level.
{{term:nelson-regel-7|Rule 7}}: 15 points in a row within 1σ (zone C) on both sides — less spread than the limits suggest, often subgroups from mixed streams or limits computed too wide.
{{term:nelson-regel-8|Rule 8}}: 8 points in a row beyond 1σ on both sides, none in zone C — a mixture of two levels, e.g. two suppliers or shifts.

blocks.content: σ is the σ̂ of the respective subchart. The individuals or X̄ chart is checked with all checked rules; its violations appear in the table and in the Violations figure.

On the MR, R and S chart only rules 1–4 apply (as in Minitab); their violations only show in that chart's badge. The dispersion statistic is skewed, so zones built from (UCL − center line)/3 would have no defined false-alarm rate there.
The rules are hints, not verdicts. Every violation should trigger a cause search, not an automatic alarm. Too many active rules create false alarms.

As in Minitab, only rule 1 is on by default. On 25 points of a stable process it falsely signals a special cause in about 7 % of cases, rules 1–6 together in about 24 %. Switch further rules on deliberately — while establishing limits, Minitab recommends rules 1, 2 and 7.

With USL and LSL ({{term:spezifikationsgrenzen|specification limits}}) the module computes the {{term:prozessfaehigkeit|process capability}} from the center line and the within spread of the first subchart.

{{term:cp|Cp}} = (USL − LSL)/(6σ), Cpu = (USL − x̄)/(3σ), Cpl = (x̄ − LSL)/(3σ), {{term:cpk|Cpk}} = min(Cpu, Cpl); with only one limit Cpk is its value and there is no Cp. x̄ is the center line of the first subchart.

σ is the within spread: MR̄/d₂ for I-MR, R̄/d₂ for X̄-R, S̄/c₄ for X̄-S. For the X̄ charts the σ̂ of the means is scaled back to individual values by √n. With stages the center line and σ of the last stage apply, with frozen limits the frozen values. If σ̂ = 0 there is no capability.

The Cpk figure is green (capable) from 1.33, yellow (conditionally capable) from 1.0, red below. Cp and Cpk with the within spread show what the process can do in the short term; the overall spread across all values ({{term:ppk|Ppk}}) is computed by the module Process Capability. Capability indices are only meaningful for a stable process: stabilize the chart first, then read Cpk.

blocks.term: Spec limits instead of control limits
blocks.content: {{term:spezifikationsgrenzen|USL/LSL}} come from the customer, {{term:regelgrenze|UCL/LCL}} from process data. Mixing them (drawing spec limits on the chart and treating them as control limits) is among the most common SPC mistakes. On X̄ charts the specification lines sit next to means, which spread less than individual values: a mean within the specification does not mean all individual values are within it.
Applying an I-MR chart to proportion data or a p-chart to individual measurements yields nonsense limits. Data type and subgroup structure must fit the chart type.
With 5 subgroups the limits are unstable and keep shifting. At least 20–25 subgroups are needed for a reliable baseline.
Every extra rule increases the false-alarm rate. Enabling all {{term:nelson-regeln|Nelson rules}} gives a “hit” every few points on average, and the team stops taking the chart seriously.
Pulling limits along with every violation hides the drift. Only adjust limits when there is a documented reason (new process, new equipment).

blocks.term: Exclusion on X̄ charts hits a different subgroup
blocks.content: On X̄-R and X̄-S the dialog takes the number of the clicked subgroup, but the computation reads it as the number of an individual value and excludes the subgroup that contains this value. Example with n = 5: an exclusion at subgroup #3 takes subgroup #1 out of the limits (it contains the third individual value), and the gray ✕ appears there; subgroup #3 stays in the computation. Before excluding on an X̄ chart, check where the ✕ appears and compare the limits.

The Phase II badge and the button only follow the stored limits. After a change of chart type or subgroup size, or with stages, it still reads “Phase II (frozen)”, but the chart computes live with new limits. Switching back makes the frozen limits apply again. To really start over, thaw the limits before switching.

blocks.term: Dashboard tile computes differently from the module
blocks.content: The dashboard tile computes without stages, without excluded points and without frozen limits, checks the rules over the whole series and computes Cpk over all values. With stages, exclusions or Phase II it therefore shows a different center line, limits, violations and Cpk than the module. The module is authoritative; the tile is an overview.
A control chart without a defined reaction procedure is decoration. Per violation, it must be clear: who looks, who decides, who documents.
